title: ETSI Identifies Technical Limitations and Implementation Vulnerabilities in Quantum Random Number Generators (ETSI TR 104 171) - Quantum Computing Report
gist: ETSI TC CYBER published TR 104 171, QRNG implementation guidelines warning that hardware flaws, detector dead time, thermal noise and side channels can make quantum random number generators predictable, and introducing an Entropy Zero Trust framework plus trust-level, throughput and power classifications ahead of normative specs tied to FIPS 140-3/Common Criteria and PQC.

insights.claim: ETSI TR 104 171 warns that although quantum processes are non-deterministic, practical QRNG hardware effects such as detector dead times, thermal noise and side-channel leakage can reintroduce predictability into outputs unless audited and conditioned.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: 'Quantum' does not equal secure by default; QRNG vendors face a higher assurance bar and buyers will demand audited entropy.

insights.claim: Named QRNG attack vectors include optical-injection 'blinding' of photodetectors, RF electromagnetic interference and power-analysis probing; mitigations include optical isolators, EMI/magnetic shielding, voltage monitoring and continuous statistical sampling at 1 Hz or faster.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Hardening requirements add cost and engineering burden, favoring QRNG vendors with mature hardware security.

insights.claim: ETSI's Entropy Zero Trust (EZT) framework treats every stage of the entropy pipeline as untrusted, requiring continuous hardware verification, runtime attestation and cryptographic signing, with a hardware root of trust (TPM/eFuse) for boot attestation.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: EZT compliance is likely to become a procurement checkbox for QRNG products in telecom and government.

insights.claim: TR 104 171 defines QRNG trust levels from TL-0 (raw unverified source) through TL-2 (EZT-compliant platform) to TL-3 (critical/military grade), throughput classes from Class I (≤100k) to Class V (≥1G), and power classes from Class A (≤100 mW) to Class D (2-10 W).
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: A classification matrix enables product segmentation and comparable spec sheets across QRNG vendors.

insights.claim: The guidelines span the full QRNG lifecycle: physical modeling of the quantum entropy source, real-time conditional min-entropy estimation, randomness extraction via seeded Toeplitz hashing or multi-source extractors, health monitoring and tamper resistance.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: Defines the engineering checklist QRNG products will be judged against.

insights.claim: ETSI outlined priorities for follow-on normative Technical Specifications covering standardized API command sets, logging protocols, Common Criteria/FIPS 140-3 alignment, and integrating certified QRNG entropy pools with PQC standards ML-KEM and ML-DSA.
insights.speaker: Mohamed Abdel-Kareem
insights.so_what: QRNG is being positioned as a complement to PQC migration; certification alignment will gate QRNG adoption in regulated markets.
